To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prenatal exposure to vitamin D may not influence the risk of fracture in childhood, regardless of whether the mother was pregnant during the period of vitamin D fortification.
the association between prenatal low vitamin D and risk of fractures was not modified by season of birth, but was attenuated by period effects.
the risk of fractures was not reduced by the vitamin D fortication of margarine in late childhood, and that the risk of fracture was not influenced by season of birth in this age group.

whether prenatal exposure to extra maternal vitamin D from a nationwide mandatory fortification programme in Denmark of 1·5 µg vitamin D per 100 g of margarine was associated with fracture risk in late childhood, irrespective of the season of birth.
the effect of prenatal exposure to vitamin D on fracture risk in late childhood.
the association between prenatal exposure to vitamin D and risk of fractures during adolescence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prenatal exposure to vitamin D is probably not associated with fracture risk in late childhood.
prenatal vitamin D fortification does not influence fracture risk in children.
the results of this study are not sufficient to conclude that prenatal exposure to vitamin D has a protective effect on bone health in late childhood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of fractures was higher among children born in Denmark before 1985, compared with children born in 1985 and later.

we have shown that prenatal vitamin D fortification of margarine in Denmark during 1 year did not influence fracture risk among 10–17-year-old children, and that the association between season of birth, prenatal vitamin D availability and fracture risk is unlikely.
prenatal low vitamin D may not have consequences for bone development in late childhood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of prenatal vitamin D on fracture risk is likely to be small.
the effect of a prenatal intervention may not be evident until many years later.
there is no evidence that prenatal vitamin D exposure from mandatory fortification is associated with fractures in childhood.
